texts.value: Catalyzes the reduction of FMN to FMNH2 which is used to reduce pyrimidine by RutA via the Rut pathway. In vitro, the flavin reductase Fre can substitute for the function of RutF, however, RutF is required for uracil utilization in vivo

Catalyzes the pyrimidine ring opening between N-3 and C-4 by an unusual flavin hydroperoxide-catalyzed mechanism, adding oxygen atoms in the process to yield ureidoacrylate peracid, that immediately reacts with FMN forming ureidoacrylate and FMN-N(5)-oxide. The FMN-N(5)-oxide reacts spontaneously with NADH to produce FMN. Requires the flavin reductase RutF to regenerate FMN in vivo. RutF can be substituted by Fre in vitro

texts.value: Hydrolyzes ureidoacrylate to form aminoacrylate and carbamate. The carbamate hydrolyzes spontaneously, thereby releasing one of the nitrogen atoms of the pyrimidine ring as ammonia and one of its carbon atoms as CO2

Involved in pyrimidine catabolism (PubMed:16540542). Catalyzes the deamination of 3-aminoacrylate to malonic semialdehyde, a reaction that can also occur spontaneously (PubMed:33839153). RutC may facilitate the reaction and modulate the metabolic fitness, rather than catalyzing essential functions (PubMed:33839153). In vitro, can also deaminate 2-aminoacrylate (PubMed:33839153)

NADP-dependent dehydrogenase with broad substrate specificity acting on 3-hydroxy acids (PubMed:12535615, PubMed:21349860). Catalyzes the NADP-dependent oxidation of L-allo-threonine to L-2-amino-3-keto-butyrate, which is spontaneously decarboxylated into aminoacetone (PubMed:12535615). The highest catalytic efficiency is observed with L-allo-threonine, but the enzyme also acts in vitro on D-threonine, L-serine, D-serine, D-3-hydroxyisobutyrate, L-3-hydroxyisobutyrate, D-glycerate and L-glycerate (PubMed:12535615, PubMed:21349860). It cannot use L-threonine, D-allo-threonine, DL-threo-3-phenyl-serine, malonate, DL-malate, citrate, isocitrate, DL-lactate, DL-tartrate, gluconate, glycerol or glycolate (PubMed:12535615). It is specific for NADP(+) and cannot use NAD(+) (PubMed:12535615). In addition, is able to detoxify malonic semialdehyde (3-oxopropanoate) by catalyzing the reduction of malonic semialdehyde to 3-hydroxypropionic acid (PubMed:20400551). This function overlaps with that of RutE, as both enzymes can reduce malonic semialdehyde to 3-hydroxypropionic acid, and YdfG is likely to be involved in the Rut pathway for pyrimidine degradation under certain circumstances (PubMed:20400551)

May reduce toxic product malonic semialdehyde to 3-hydroxypropionic acid, which is excreted. RutE is apparently supplemented by YdfG. Required in vivo, but not in vitro in pyrimidine nitrogen degradation

<comment datatype="string"><b>General Background</b>
<p>
Pyrimidine nucleotides can be catabolized through three different pathways. The best characterized is the reductive pathway (see <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=PWY-6430">thymine degradation</a> and <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=PWY-3982">uracil degradation I (reductive)</a>), in which the pyrimidine nucleotides are reduced to <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=Beta-amino-acids">a &beta; amino acid</a>, <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CARBON-DIOXIDE">CO<SUB>2</SUB></a> and <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=AMMONIA">ammonia</a>. The pathway is found in mammals, plants, some fungi and microorganisms [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/13428755">Fritzson57</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/13416173">Campbell57</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16655478">Evans61</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16656066">Tsai65</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10656811">Gojkovic00</a>]. The oxidative pathway (see <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=PWY-6426">uracil degradation II (oxidative)</a>) is only found in a few bacterial species and has not been characterized nearly as well. In it uracil is converted to <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=UREA">urea</a> and <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=MALONATE">malonate</a> via <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=BARBITURATE">barbiturate</a> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12981104">Hayaishi52</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14955523">Lara52</a>]. A third pathway, known as the Rut pathway, was discovered much later in <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ORGANISM&object=TAX-562"><i>Escherichia coli</i></a> and other bacteria and is described here.
<p>
<b>About This Pathway</b>
<p>
<a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ORGANISM&object=TAX-562"><i>Escherichia coli</i></a> is able to utilize pyrimidine nucleosides and bases as the sole source of nitrogen at room temperature.  This novel pathway for pyrimidine degradation was discovered by a combination of functional and comparative genomics techniques including high-throughput microarray and phenotype analysis [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16540542">Loh06</a>].
<p>
In the presence of a flavin reductase, <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=G6523-MONOMER">pyrimidine oxygenase</a> catalyzes the first step in this pathway, the ring opening of uracil at the C4 carbonyl by a novel flavin hydroperoxide-catalyzed mechanism.  The initial product of the reaction appears to be <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD0-2338">ureidoacrylate peracid</a>, which is unstable and converts to ureidoacrylate either enzymatically or spontaneously [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20369853">Mukherjee10</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20400551">Kim10c</a>].  <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=G6522-MONOMER">Ureidoacrylate amido hydrolase</a> then hydrolyzes <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD0-2331">3-ureidoacrylate</a>, yielding carbamate and aminoacrylate.  In spontaneous reactions, these compounds liberate one molecule of <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=AMMONIA">ammonia</a> each, which serves as the utilizable source of nitrogen.  The remaining carbon compounds, CO<sub>2</sub> and <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=MALONATE-S-ALD">malonate semialdehyde</a>, can not be utilized.  In fact, malonic semialdehyde must be detoxified by one of two malonic semialdehyde reductases to <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=3-HYDROXY-PROPIONATE">3-hydroxypropionate</a>, which is then excreted into the medium.  The toxicity of malonic semialdehyde appears to limit growth on pyrimidines as the sole source of nitrogen.
<p>
Additional enzymes encoded by the <i>rut</i> operon of <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ORGANISM&object=TAX-562"><i>Escherichia coli</i></a> may catalyze one or more of the spontaneous reactions of this pathway and serve to detoxify pathway intermediates or side products [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20400551">Kim10c</a>].
<p>
Reviews: [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16595627">Osterman06</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17555842">Piskur07</a>]
<p>
</comment>
</Pathway>
